title: Can You Use Sewing Thread for Cross Stitch? What Changes

seo.title: Can You Use Sewing Thread for Cross Stitch? What Changes
seo.meta_description: Learn whether ordinary sewing thread can be used for cross stitch, how it differs from embroidery floss, and how fabric count, coverage and color matching change.
seo.search_intent: People wondering whether ordinary sewing thread can replace embroidery floss in cross stitch and what practical differences to expect.

excerpt: A practical guide to using sewing thread for cross stitch, including thickness, coverage, fabric count, color matching and when the substitution works.
content_html:
Embroidery floss is the standard choice for counted cross stitch, but it is not the only thread that can physically make a cross. Ordinary sewing thread can be used on Aida or evenweave if you understand how its thickness, twist and surface differ from stranded embroidery cotton. The main question is not whether the stitch is possible, but whether the result will have the coverage, texture and handling you want.

Why embroidery floss is usually easier for cross stitch

Stranded embroidery floss is designed to be separated into individual strands, which makes it easy to adjust coverage for different fabric counts. Six-strand cotton can become one, two or three strands without changing the basic color or finish. It is also relatively soft, so multiple strands can spread across the surface of a cross instead of behaving like one tight cord.

Most cross stitch patterns also assume this kind of thread when they list strand counts and color references. If a chart says to use two strands on 14-count Aida, that instruction is normally based on embroidery floss rather than all-purpose sewing thread. Replacing the material therefore changes more than the brand: you are changing the diameter and construction of every stitch.

What changes when you use ordinary sewing thread

All-purpose sewing thread is generally much thinner than a strand of embroidery floss and is often more tightly twisted. A single sewing thread can look extremely fine on standard Aida, leaving far more fabric visible than expected. Using several lengths together may increase coverage, but a bundle of tightly twisted threads does not necessarily spread in the same flat way as stranded cotton.

The surface can also look different. Polyester sewing thread may have more shine and spring than cotton floss, while cotton sewing thread can look matte and crisp. Neither effect is automatically wrong. It simply means the finished design may look more like fine linework or miniature embroidery than a conventional soft, full cross stitch.

Fabric count determines whether the substitution works

Very fine thread makes more sense on high-count evenweave or linen, where each cross is tiny and bulky floss can become crowded. On 28-, 32- or higher-count fabrics stitched over one, a fine sewing or machine embroidery thread may produce a clean result. On 11- or 14-count Aida, the same thread may look too sparse unless several strands are combined.

Do a small coverage test before committing to a large design. Stitch ten or twenty crosses with the number of sewing threads you are considering, then view them from normal distance. Check whether the fabric shows through, whether the holes feel crowded and whether the bundle twists or knots. A test patch answers these questions more reliably than trying to convert strand counts mathematically.

Color matching can be harder than the stitching itself

A cross stitch chart built around DMC or another embroidery system gives you repeatable color numbers and families. General sewing thread is sold for a different purpose, so an exact equivalent may not exist. Even if two spools look similar under indoor light, their undertone and sheen can behave differently when stitched in a block next to neighboring colors.

This matters most in shaded designs, portraits and projects with many close color changes. For a monochrome motif, lettering or a simple geometric piece, exact conversion may be less important. If you substitute sewing thread in a multi-color chart, compare the whole palette together rather than matching each spool separately in isolation.

When sewing thread can be a useful creative choice

Fine thread can be useful for delicate backstitch, tiny details, blackwork-style lines or miniature work where ordinary floss feels too heavy. It can also be an intentional design choice when you want a sharper, more graphic line. Machine embroidery thread can create a particularly smooth or shiny surface, although its slipperiness may require shorter lengths and more careful tension.

For experimentation, start with a small project rather than a large full-coverage chart. Keep the thread lengths comfortable, let the needle untwist regularly and avoid forcing a very large bundle through Aida holes simply to imitate two-strand floss. If four or five fine threads are needed for acceptable coverage, using actual embroidery floss may be easier and more consistent.

How to decide whether to use it for a full project

Ask three questions: does the thread cover the fabric well, does it pass through the holes without excessive friction, and can you reproduce the colors you need? If the answer to all three is yes, there is no technical rule preventing you from stitching the project with sewing thread. Cross stitch is defined by the counted X-shaped stitch, not by one compulsory fiber.

For predictable results, especially from a PDF pattern that specifies strand counts and named colors, embroidery floss remains the simpler choice. Sewing thread works best when you are intentionally changing the look, stitching on very fine fabric or testing a small design where exact color conversion is not critical. Treat it as a material substitution that deserves a sample, not as a one-for-one replacement with identical behavior.
